rationale: A richly detailed and coherent vignette that traces a clear internal logic from the witnessed medical near-loss of her son through the development of dismissal-based injustice appraisals, sensory triggers (blood, needles, medical objects), fragmented emotional memory (affect without image), and maintaining strategies (emotional suppression, reassurance-seeking, avoidance of positive affect). The phlebotomy scene provides a concrete functional impairment that motivates help-seeking. Particularly strong on Ehlers-Clark mechanisms — the disjointed memory with detached affective intrusions is unusually well rendered.

The vignette is vivid, well-written, and covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers-Clark components with concrete sensory detail (fragmented memory of diesel/sand/metal, narrow-road avoidance, motorcycle backfire trigger, "always braced"). However, it leans toward comprehensive symptom coverage rather than tracing a tight idiosyncratic mechanism — the link between her auditor-precision identity and her shame at "small mistakes" is hinted at but not fully developed into a maintenance cycle. The mention of cultural reserve adds texture but is only loosely tied to maintaining factors, slightly diluting clinical focus.

This vignette is exceptionally rich and coherent: the trauma, the sensory-based intrusion (rust, wet concrete, rain, the diminutive name), the avoidance (makeup, clothing, distraction), the negative appraisals (body untrustworthy, self diminished), and the hyperarousal all interlock with clear internal logic. The Ehlers & Clark mechanisms are explicitly shown — including the dissociative quality of the memory ("belongs to another woman") combined with vivid sensory re-experiencing, and the way maintenance strategies narrow her life (declined promotions). A trainee could trace exactly why this person has PTSD in this particular way.

The vignette presents a richly detailed, internally coherent case showing how Mona's specific role (matching dog tags to names) shapes her survivor guilt, her choice of auditing as a profession, and her control rituals. All DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers-Clark components are explicitly shown — diesel smell as a trigger, the binder-drop dissociative "glitch," the bulletproof glass metaphor for numbing, and the way her fortress-building maintains rather than resolves the trauma. The narrative traces a clear line from trauma to belief ("the world is fundamentally unsafe") to behavior (mapped exits, missing her daughter's games) to maintenance cycle.

This is a richly detailed, internally coherent vignette that traces a clear logic from trauma (the stairwell entrapment with associated bodily sensations) through specific maladaptive strategies (stopping exercise, exit-scanning, perimeter walks) to their maintaining effect on hypervigilance — an excellent teaching example of an Ehlers-Clark maintenance cycle. The nephew incident anchors functional impairment vividly, and emotional numbing/pushing away positive emotions is well shown. Notable gaps: explicit intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares) are not described — the trauma is "vivid" in recall but no Criterion B re-experiencing is shown — and the nature of the trauma memory (fragmented/present-tense) is not addressed.

The vignette covers most DSM and Ehlers-Clark domains with some specific sensory details (metallic taste, neck pain as somatic trigger, derealization of memory). However, hyperarousal is only loosely implied through workplace stressors rather than explicit hypervigilance/startle/sleep disturbance. The prose drifts into generic recovery-narrative language ("flicker of hope," "determined to find a path forward") that reads more like a case summary than a lived clinical picture, weakening the internal logic linking trauma → belief → behavior.

A coherent, well-constructed vignette that traces a clear line from the index event (crowd surge in an aid site where threat and helper were indistinguishable) to the specific belief that safety is conditional, to the behaviors (exit-scanning, avoiding exercise, shutting down positive affect) that maintain hyperarousal. Particularly strong on Ehlers-Clark mechanisms — appraisals, current threat, maladaptive strategies (avoiding exertion because interoceptive cues mimic alarm; suppressing relaxation), and triggers. Notable gap: no explicit intrusion symptoms (nightmares, flashbacks, distress at reminders) and no description of fragmented/nowness memory, so Criterion B and ec_memory are not met.

The vignette establishes a clear internal logic linking somatic sensations (neck pain, nausea) from the entrapment to current triggers, dissociative memory quality, and negative appraisals about belonging and trust. Strong on Ehlers-Clark mechanisms — particularly somatic triggers, sense of current threat, and dissociative memory quality. Weaknesses: avoidance (Criterion C) is not clearly shown beyond general withdrawal, and maladaptive coping strategies are not explicitly described — we see triggers and arousal but not what Linh does to manage them. Some phrasing ("solidify a pervasive dread") feels slightly constructed rather than observed.

This vignette is exemplary: it traces a clear internal logic from the IED incident through the fragmented memory, survivor guilt, and the appraisal "I am the kind of person who fails when it matters most" to the specific avoidance and hypervigilant behaviors (corner office, ground-floor apartment, declining mentorship). Triggers (perfume, fire alarm), fragmented memory, current threat sense, and maladaptive strategies (constant scanning as protective) are all shown with concrete idiosyncratic detail. Every element connects to the maintenance cycle, and the closing reflection about wondering whether the threat is real captures the Ehlers & Clark framework beautifully.

A richly detailed vignette that traces the link between a fragmented, disorganised memory and Tane's specific triggers (slamming doors, crying babies, sudden peripheral movement) and avoidance strategies (moving to the stockroom, delegating to his wife). The full DSM-5 picture is shown rather than listed, and the Ehlers & Clark mechanisms—fragmented memory, sense of current threat at the register, negative appraisal about institutional failure, hypervigilant scanning as maladaptive strategy—are explicit. Numbing is shown both in his wife's observation and his own "flat and empty" self-description, giving the case unusual coherence.

A richly detailed, coherent vignette that traces the line from a specific traumatic event (bombing, four-hour entrapment) through intrusive nightmares of the welded-shut storage room, concrete triggers (fireworks, car backfire), avoidance and rigid routines, and a clear appraisal that "safety is no longer something he can feel, only something he can construct." The mechanism — that control rituals substitute for an internal sense of safety — is a teachable, non-obvious clinical insight. Minor weakness: the mention of his deceased wife adds atmosphere but is not fully integrated into the PTSD maintenance picture, slightly diluting g4.

A richly detailed, decades-long PTSD presentation grounded in a specific workplace shooting witnessed forty years ago, with the trauma memory still arriving as vivid sensory fragments (linoleum shade, smell of ozone and copper). The vignette shows a clear internal logic: return to the register as an attempt to rebuild order, avoidance routes through the service entrance, hypervigilant scanning of hands and jackets, and a present-day trigger (cracker box) that re-activates the full arousal response. Minor weakness is that the "Oceania heritage" line adds atmosphere without clear clinical function, but otherwise every detail serves the maintenance picture.

A richly detailed, internally coherent vignette that traces the line from a specific betrayal trauma to fragmented memory, to interoceptive triggers (his own racing heart), to avoidance of law enforcement contexts, to the injustice appraisal that maintains the symptoms. The "friendly fire" by a trusted colleague gives a distinctive clinical signature — the betrayal appraisal is shown to be a maintaining factor, not just background. All DSM-5 and Ehlers-Clark elements are explicit and shown in action rather than merely named.

A rich, specific narrative grounded in concrete sensory and cognitive detail — the taste of brackish water returning in the present, somatic vigilance about neck aches and feeling unwell, and the depersonalization-like sense that the event "belonged to someone else." It traces a clear internal logic from trauma to fragmented memory to body-based triggers to isolating appraisals about being unknowable to others. Minor weakness: hyperarousal beyond somatic checking (e.g., sleep, startle) is less developed, but Criterion E is met through body hypervigilance and reactivity to reminders.

A well-constructed, coherent vignette of witnessing-trauma PTSD in an older adult, with specific concrete detail (loud-voiced young men in the shop, facing the entrance, losing track of numbers at the till) and clear DSM-5 and Ehlers-Clark coverage. The internal logic — shame at freezing fueling negative self-appraisal, which deepens isolation and avoidance — is traceable throughout. Slightly less novel in clinical teaching value because the maintenance cycles, while present, follow a fairly familiar pattern rather than offering an unexpected nuance.

A richly detailed, narratively coherent vignette of a torture survivor with PTSD. Specific sensory triggers (pneumatic presses syncing with heartbeat, grease feeling like dried blood, mop bucket flinch) clearly demonstrate trauma cues, intrusive sensory memory, and current threat. The internal logic — why she chose factory work, why she divorced, why she sleeps with a knife — connects trauma to belief to behaviour to maintaining cycles with unusual depth.

Vivid, well-written narrative with concrete sensory triggers (scent of rain, car backfires, back alley) and clear DSM-5 coverage including avoidance, hypervigilance, intrusion (nightmare of alley becoming corridor), and functional impairment at work and intimacy. The internal logic is mostly visible — mugging led to threat-monitoring at work, intimacy, and family contact — though the connection between specific beliefs and behaviors is more shown than analyzed. Some details (Middle Eastern family, age 26) add color but do not deeply connect to maintaining mechanisms, and the literary tone occasionally prioritizes atmosphere over clinical clarity.

This vignette demonstrates exceptional internal coherence — you can trace the line from the assault, to the fragmented frozen-frame memory, to the guilt-saturated appraisals, to the punishment-logic strategies (food restriction, refusal to rest) that prevent memory processing, to the hypervigilance that the strategies maintain. Each Ehlers & Clark component is explicitly shown with specific detail (the "thick, suspended, wrong" silence as trigger; relaxation experienced as exposure; the mutual reinforcement of threat and appraisal). The freezing in the storage room doorway concretely anchors functional impairment, and the disclosed shame to her husband adds clinically rich detail about social withdrawal without being extraneous.

The vignette explicitly covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers-Clark components, with notable specificity around the rigid eating control as a maladaptive coping strategy and the snapshot-like quality of the memory. However, it is severely repetitive — the same points about eating restriction, route planning, and self-blame are restated 4-5 times each, which obscures clarity and reads as padded rather than crafted. The internal logic (assault → guilt/self-blame → control via restriction → reinforced threat) is visible, but the constant restating dilutes rather than deepens it.

The vignette covers all DSM-5 PTSD criteria explicitly — witnessing the shooting, intrusive replay, nightmares, avoidance of community events and fishing, guilt and isolation, sleep disturbance, and clear functional impairment. It also shows triggers (distressed parolees morphing into the victim's face), maladaptive coping (throwing himself into work to suppress memories), and a guilt-laden appraisal. However, the writing is somewhat literary and atmospheric ("shadows loom large," "fragility of life") rather than rooted in idiosyncratic clinical detail, and the internal logic linking belief → behavior → maintenance is only partially developed. Current threat sense is not clearly shown.

The vignette explicitly names PTSD components (triggers, fragmented memory, hypervigilance, negative appraisals) and shows their interplay, which aids learning. However, it is repetitive and somewhat formulaic, restating the same cycle multiple times rather than building a vivid personal narrative. Intrusion symptoms (flashbacks/nightmares) and clear avoidance behaviors are notably absent, and maladaptive coping strategies are not specifically depicted.

The vignette traces a clear and coherent line from the assault to specific beliefs (world is dangerous, self is broken, cannot trust own judgment), to behaviours (compulsive scanning, avoidance, overcompliance), to maintaining cycles (avoidance confirms danger; scanning reinforces threat; rumination sharpens the memory). Concrete sensory detail (cologne triggers in the clinic, the paper bag with sparrow supplies) anchors it in lived experience, and the Ehlers-Clark maintenance loops are explicitly named. A minor weakness is that the maintenance mechanisms are sometimes spelled out almost didactically, which slightly nudges it toward instructional rather than purely narrative writing, but the depth and internal logic are excellent.

This vignette is clear, well-structured, and explicitly demonstrates all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers-Clark components, with concrete triggers (gunshot sounds, uniforms, military talk), a vividly described "happening now" memory quality, self-blame appraisals, and maladaptive strategies (carrying a weapon, avoidance). The clinical picture is grounded and recognizable. However, the internal logic is only partially developed — we see what Armando does and that it maintains his vigilance, but the specific link between his dentist identity, his prior sense of safety, and why these particular triggers carry the weight they do is not deeply drawn, leaving it somewhat closer to a thorough symptom illustration than a fully mechanistic case formulation.

The vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers-Clark components explicitly, with concrete triggers (olfactory cues, footsteps, shadows) and a clear maintaining cycle (avoidance via overwork, fawning). However, the writing is somewhat formulaic and ends with a summary paragraph that reads like a checklist rather than a narrative. Some clinical labels (e.g., "fawning", "magical thinking") are inserted didactically rather than emerging organically from the patient's experience.

The vignette is rich, specific, and covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components with concrete sensory detail (smell of antiseptic mingling with phantom smoke, the dental drill triggering startle). It depicts a chronic, late-life trajectory with grief compounding numbing, which is clinically valuable. However, the internal logic linking trauma → specific beliefs → maintaining behaviors is only partly developed; we see avoidance and overwork as comfort but less about the specific beliefs that sustain the cycle, making it more illustrative than mechanistically instructive.

A well-constructed vignette with a clear internal logic linking institutional betrayal to negative appraisals, avoidance, and hypervigilance. The fragmented memory, specific triggers (police stations, workplace stress, unusual silence), and maintaining behaviors (route avoidance, social withdrawal) are explicitly shown. Whether Criterion A is strictly met is debatable — being shoved and verbally threatened may not constitute the DSM-5 threshold of "actual or threatened death/serious injury/sexual violence" — but it is at least arguably present.

The vignette covers all DSM-5 criteria and Ehlers & Clark components, with specific triggers (blood, needles, drips) and a clear precipitating event (customer with medical equipment). However, it reads more like a theoretical exposition of the Ehlers & Clark model than a personal narrative—repeatedly naming "negative appraisals," "maladaptive strategies," and "cycle of threat" rather than showing them. The repetition and meta-commentary about cycles weaken the narrative flow and make it feel formulaic rather than clinically observed.

This vignette presents a nuanced and less typical PTSD presentation — trauma from witnessing a child's life-threatening illness — with rich specificity (hospital corridors, language difficulty under fear, the phone in hand). The internal logic is tightly traced: from the helplessness of watching her son's body fail, to her present-day catastrophising about loved ones' minor symptoms, to her shifted worldview ("a person who is always waiting for bad news"). All DSM criteria and E&C components are shown in action through concrete behaviours (ambulance freezing, avoiding hospital district, hypervigilant calls to son) rather than just named. Particularly valuable for teaching is how the survival outcome paradoxically isolates her grief and maintains the threat sense.

A richly drawn vignette that illustrates PTSD arising from a prolonged medical caregiving trauma — an under-recognised but clinically important presentation. The internal logic is fully traceable: the threat that "never resolved" emotionally despite the son's survival, the sensory triggers (refrigerator hum, rubbing alcohol, vinyl chairs) tied to specific hospital memories, the silent avoidance maintained by cultural stoicism and concealment from her husband. Every detail serves the clinical picture, and the final line ("waiting for news that will never come") captures the frozen sense of current threat that defines the Ehlers-Clark model.

The vignette traces a clear internal logic from trauma to fragmented memory to appraisals of institutional failure and personal defectiveness, and shows how hypervigilance and triggers maintain the conviction of ongoing danger. DSM-5 Criterion C (avoidance) is notably absent — Kahu remains in public-facing work and there is no clear behavioural or cognitive avoidance described, which is a meaningful gap. Some phrasing leans toward literary rather than observed-clinical detail, but the case is coherent, specific, and explicit about most PTSD features.
